notes.1a: (i) Quite a number of candidates considered water as a solvent rather than a reactant. Many wrongly thought that propanone served as a reactant. Only a few realised that the water could act as another nucleophile leading to an alcohol. There were many irrelevant statements e.g. ‘Dry propanone will not react with the bromoalkane or halide’, ‘propanone acts as a catalyst’ or ‘bromine is usually a liquid’.
notes.1aii: The essence of this question was to relate the data to the high yield in the reaction. It was insufficient to say the position of the equilibrium was to the right – the question essentially states that already. The equilibrium shift to the right is driven by the sodium bromide precipitating out of solution due to its low solubility. Many candidates concentrated on the relative solubilities of the bromide and the iodide driving the equilibrium rather than the precipitation of one. Some candidates suggested that a high concentration of sodium iodide would push the reaction but there was no evidence of such a concentration in the question, only the low solubility of the sodium bromide (from precipitation) that would lead to a low equilibrium concentration of sodium bromide. Many candidates resorted to bond lengths, strength or energy or compound stability, which provided no answer.
notes.1b: Many candidates found this challenging and list answers were common here. Some candidates offered a precaution that did not match their explanation e.g. ‘use a fume cupboard’ incorrectly linked to compound ‘flammability’. Sometimes the generic descriptions ‘harmful’ or ‘damaging’ were used instead of a specific term such as ‘irritating’. Some candidates included ‘toxic’ or ‘explosive’, �PAGE�45 9701 Chemistry November 2018 which are not in the given list of hazards. ‘Heat’ is not the same as a naked flame nor is ‘keep away from flammable materials’. Many candidates stated ‘gloves’ and ‘goggles’, which were expressly excluded in the question. Also excluded were masks, as the question excluded protective equipment.
notes.1c: (i) This was a straightforward calculation, requiring correctly quoting to two decimal places, at which virtually all candidates succeeded.
notes.1cii: In order to assess the effect of the concentration of one reactant all the other variables need to be kept constant; many candidates did not recognise this. Most candidates correctly varied the volume of sodium iodide; many also wrongly varied the volume of 1-bromopropane. Others did not realise that the propanone volume needed to change in order to maintain a constant volume – essential in this type of experiment. Some had 50cm3 of sodium iodide, which would exceed the 42cm3 total volume limit.
notes.1iii: Most candidates identified time as the dependent variable.
notes.1iv: Most candidates also identified the reciprocal of time as a measure of the rate of reaction. Rate expressions that did not assume first order were also accepted.
notes.1v: The major source of error is determining the time at which the cross can no longer be seen. Volumetric limitations were suggested but were not significant as were ‘not all the reactants were used up’. Some ingenious improvements were seen involving video recordings and colorimeters. Doing repeats does not improve accuracy, since each repeat would be subject to the same limits of accuracy. Suggestions such as ‘stir’, ‘use an indicator’ or ‘heat it up’ were irrelevant.
notes.1d: This question proved to be challenging to the majority of the candidates and confused answers were common. It was not widely known that in an S 1 reaction the rate determining step does not involve NaI but in an S 2 it does. Some candidates thought there were two different rates in conflict or that the two rates were different. The tendency was to resort to a general rate statement, stereochemistry or other things to do with nucleophilic substitutions.
notes.2a: (i) The realistic way of maintaining a set temperature is by way of a water bath set at 40°C. Temperature controlled immersion heaters were also accepted. Devices such as incubators or calibrated thermometers, which are impractical, or room temperature control (inefficient) were not accepted.
notes.2aii: Many confused answers were seen in response to this question. A variety of reasons were given such as the ions move faster, a movement of electrons or temperature change (the question stated the temperature was maintained at 40°C). The temperature at 40°C would evaporate some of the water solvent leading to a change in silver ion concentration.
notes.2b: Most candidates correctly calculated the values to two decimal places. A common error was quoting 1.00 as 1.0, giving the last three values in –log [Ag+(aq)] to three decimal places and missing the negative sign in –0.18. A few miscalculated the values in the final column producing values that were out of the scale range on the grid. In this situation, candidates should be advised to recalculate the values.
notes.2c: (i) The plotting of the data was done very well, with only a handful of candidates misplotting. The plotted points were indistinct in some responses. Sometimes the –0.18 value was plotted as positive and –2.56 as –2.60. The straight-line plot was very well done. �PAGE�46
notes.2cii: Candidates who had plotted their points correctly could easily identify the anomalous point above the line. Deducing a reason proved more challenging. Many candidates realised that concentration must be involved but non-specific answers such as ‘The concentration is incorrect...’ were seen. Other irrelevant suggestions were seen, such as ‘voltmeter error’, ‘reading taken too late/soon’, ‘reading taken too slow’, ‘silver concentration wrong’ and ‘the temperature changed’.
notes.2iii: Most of the candidates realised that the value for log C would be the value on the y-axis, where sat the plotted line crosses a vertical grid line at a value of zero on the –log [Ag+(aq)] axis. Many candidates were able to get the correct value of –4.55 at that condition. A similar number of candidates gave a value of –5.05, which is where the line crosses the axis at the edge of the grid (–0.5 on the –log [Ag+(aq)] axis). Some candidates calculated a gradient. As the question asks ‘Use your graph and equation...’, reading two co-ordinates from the line and substituting into the equation was accepted provided the co-ordinates were on the line.
notes.2d: (i) This straightforward calculation caused few problems to the candidates.
notes.2dii: A burette or a graduated pipette are the only realistic answers. Pipettes (alone) are not available to measure 12.5cm3 and measuring cylinders are unsuitable for that volume in that volumetric context.
notes.2e: (i) Many candidates used their calculators correctly to give a correct answer to three significant figures. The most common error was to use the value from (c)(iii) directly, instead of taking its inverse log into the square term. A few wrongly used natural logs. A small number used the ‘given value of –4.20.
notes.2eii: In sketch graphs illustrating a relationship between two quantities it is correct to have the independent variable on the x-axis, in this case, temperature. The accepted relationship was an increasing line or curve. As the axes had no scales, the line could be anywhere within the grid. Common errors were not labelling the axes or introducing a plateau. A number of candidates wrongly labelled the y-axis as ‘solubility’.
notes.2f: The unsuitability of a compound in a salt bridge is defined by whether it reacts with any of the other compounds present. Of the three compounds offered either of the chlorides would react with silver ions, so are not suitable. Their unsuitability also had to be defined in terms of the removal of silver ions from solution or by precipitation of silver chloride. Very often irrelevant or incorrect chemistry was given. Examples found were ‘nitrate forms a precipitate with AgCl’, ‘nitrate because it does not contain the necessary chloride’, ‘nitrate ion will be deposited at the cathode’ and ‘nitrate will react with silver chloride’. �PAGE�47
notes.key_messages:
• The practice of writing answers in pencil and then going over in ink should be discouraged as it can
make responses difficult to read.
• Candidates who perform well have good exposure to practical techniques through regular laboratory
• Candidates should avoid providing irrelevant information in their responses. This approach often leads to
answers that contradict each other.
notes.general_comments:
There was no evidence that candidates were short of time and the majority of scripts were complete. There
were few ‘no response’ answers. Some candidates need to improve the legibility of their answers. The full
mark range was seen.
Most candidates gave numerical answers to the required number of decimal places or significant figures.
There was a marked difference between numerical and chemical questions, where the numerical questions
were better answered than the chemical questions.
In some responses, there was evidence of improvement required in basic chemical knowledge.
Candidates should be discouraged from non-specific responses such as ‘The temperature was wrong’ or
‘The candidate had an incorrect concentration’.
